idiom_name: ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes (Current.user) with automatic per-request reset; Warden env for middleware
implementation_notes: Rails supplies both the container and the lifecycle: class Current < ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes with attribute :user is a thread-isolated attributes singleton that the framework resets automatically before and after each request, so one before_action assigns Current.user and guards anywhere in the request read it without parameters. In Rack middleware the same role is played by Warden's request-scoped env['warden'] (the mechanism behind devise's authenticate! helpers), which travels with the request rather than with the thread. The classic context class is unnecessary inside Rails; outside it, the minimal equivalent is a thread-local (Thread.current[:security_context]) with an ensure-block reset. Keep Current to a few top-level globals - its own documentation warns that overfilling it tangles the model layer.
code_sketch:
class Current < ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes
  attribute :user
end

# controller concern
before_action { Current.user = authenticate_from_session! }

def require_user!
  Current.user || raise(ActionController::Unauthorized)
end
pitfalls: Current is thread-isolated and reset by the Rails executor: code in a spawned Thread, a background job or an ActionCable channel must call Current.set (or receive the principal) instead of assuming the request's values.
Never store more than a few top-level per-request attributes in Current - the framework documents that controller-specific data there becomes a mess.
Current.user is only as good as the before_action order: a controller path that skips authentication reads nil, so guards must still fail closed.
